newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Palestinian businessmen to boycott economic summit.
newsitem.headline: Palestinian businessmen to boycott economic summit.

text.p: Palestinian industrialists and businessmen will boycott official representation at next week's Middle East economic conference to protest against Israeli measures strangling their economy, union members said on Monday.

Representatives of industrial, agricultural and business associations in the Palestinian self-ruled areas decided at a meeting last Wednesday not to send an official delegation to the Cairo conference to protest against Israeli policies. The conference is scheduled to start on November 12.

"All the associations have decided to boycott the Middle East economic conference in Cairo as an expression of protest against Israeli measures which had suffocated our economy and harmed our businesses," said Adnan Faramand, owner of the Arab Food Company and a member of the food manufacturers association.
"We see no reason for our participation as long as these measures are imposed and we continue to suffer from them," he told Reuters.

The Palestinian Authority is expected to attend the conference, which brings together leaders and businessmen from around the world to discuss development projects and cooperation. The conference follows two similar summits in Casablanca, Morocco and in Amman, Jordan in 1994 and 1995.
Some Palestinian private businessmen would also participate but would not be part of the official Palestinian delegation.

Businessmen said it was imperative for Palestinian President Yasser Arafat's Authority to attend to show support to Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak, who has strongly backed the PLO's position in talks with Israel.
Two months ago, Egypt threatened to cancel the conference if Israel did not make progress in peace talks.
Palestinian businessmen complain that local industries and businesses have deteriorated as a result of closures imposed regularly on the West Bank and Gaza Strip since 1994.

Israel imposed a four-month closure earlier this year after Islamic militants carried out four suicide bombings in February and March that killed 59 people. The closure has since been eased but tough restrictions remain.
Palestinian businessmen said the closures have increased unemployment in Gaza and the West Bank to over 50 percent and reduced per capita income by 35 percent.
Many industries have had to lower production or shut down and local investment dropped while political instability and uncertainty scared foreign investors.
"As a result of the closures, Palestinian goods and people don't have freedom of movement to Israel, but Israel drowns our markets with its goods," Faramand said.
"Our businesses have reached the red line. We face many problems as a result of Israeli restrictions, we can't export, import, train our people and we are losing our markets," he said.

Mazen Sinokrot, head of the food industrialists association told al-Ayyam daily newspaper on Monday that he hoped the boycott would push the conference participants to pressure Israel to lift its restrictions.

"We have problems as a result of Israeli restrictions that prevent the development of our economy and these measures scare foreign investors away," said Bashar al-Masri, director general of al-Ayyam printing company.
"How can Palestinian businessmen do business with regional companies with multi-million dollar projects when they can't even travel between their own cities and villages?" Masri said.

Businessman Khaled Oseileh, from the West Bank town of Hebron, said he would attend the conference "because I don't think it's good to completely boycott the conference. It would be good at least, and despite the difficulties we face here, to meet other regional companies and industries."
